news_list.title: Inside India newsletter: Iran war disruptions, Modi's appeal to boost India's hospitality sector
news_list.summary:
The conflict in the Middle East has affected India's economy, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi urging citizens to curb overseas travel, save fuel -- and even pause buying gold. This bleak-sounding appeal is proving to be a boon for India's domestic travel and tourism industry.

The conflict in the Middle East is causing India acute economic pain, with its currency weakening, the import bill rising, and mounting concerns over a slowdown in growth.

But there is a silver lining: the domestic tourism industry is showing signs of a boom.

Earlier this month, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi urged citizens to reduce overseas travel in an attempt to conserve India's foreign exchange reserves, under strain from a rising import bill amid a surge in global energy prices.

The Indian rupee is among the worst-performing currencies in Asia, falling over 6% year to date against the greenback, LSEG data showed. This weakening of currency, combined with inflated jet fuel prices, has also led to one of the country's major airlines, Air India, to cancel more than a quarter of its international flights between June and August.

All this coincides with the peak season for Indian tourists travelling abroad, experts told CNBC, adding that as schools remain shut for more than a month, it is easier for families to take longer holidays to escape the Indian summer heat.

Indian Hotels Company, the country's largest hospitality group and parent of luxury chain Taj Hotels, told CNBC's "Inside India" that Modi's exhortation will "benefit the domestic tourism industry."

news_list.title: How are college grads navigating the tough job market? Here's what some are doing
news_list.summary:
By Ariana Perez-Castells, The Philadelphia Inquirer

PHILADEPHIA -- Matthew Soesanto wrapped up his undergraduate biology degree at Drexel University in March and spent weeks applying to research, coding, and pharmaceutical industry jobs this spring. But he wasn't hearing back from hiring managers.

"It just feels like I'm sending applications to a black hole," said Soesanto, who will walk in Drexel's graduation in June.

It left him wondering, "Am I doing something wrong?" he said. "There's no feedback."

Soesanto is one of Philly's many graduating college students mapping out their careers in a tough job market. Budding professionals are trying to stand out from huge pools of job applicants. They're embracing the virtual aspects of a modern workplace by showing they can use AI, while also trying to make an impression in-person at networking events.

The hiring rate is down in the past two years, even flirting with Great Recession lows in recent months. Fewer employers are signing up for career fairs, and the unemployment rate for recent graduates is higher than the overall rate for all workers -- that's been the case for a few years.

"Young people are having a challenge right now entering the workforce," said Jennifer Kebea, president of Campus Philly, which works to keep students of Philadelphia colleges from leaving the area after graduation.

Employers are still hiring, said Kebea, but they're being more selective. They are increasingly looking for candidates with AI fluency and proven experience.

"This is not a Gen Z issue. It's a changing labor market," Kebea said. "Recent grads are entering a market that's more competitive, it's more skills-focused, it's more uncertain."

Drexel senior Maggie Jiang felt discouraged about the job hunt when she first started applying to positions several months ago. The marketing and organizational management double major is more optimistic now.

"I'm hearing back from more jobs," said Jiang. "There was a period where it was like, just me sitting here, hoping."

Jiang is working as a server at a Malvern restaurant, 30 to 40 hours a week, while she looks for a full-time position. She's worked in service jobs on and off since she was a freshman.

Students like Jiang who worked while completing school have a better chance of landing a full-time job post-graduation, a recent ZipRecruiter survey found.

"I'm just really thankful that a lot of the service industry hours don't start until later in the day," she said. She finished homework during breaks between classes.

Jiang completed high school online during the pandemic. The virtual setting sapped her motivation. So she would prefer a job with some in-person work and opportunities for direct feedback, where she's not just messaging colleagues online.

"I personally can't function just being remote only," she said. "I'd rather be surrounded by a more lively environment with my coworkers."

New Temple University graduate Jaiden Charles said "hybrid is the golden option," although she's open to jobs with other setups.

Charles, who studied public relations and digital marketing in school, works remotely 20 hours a week with 1824, Universal Music Group's marketing and content strategy arm. She's been doing the job since her junior year, juggling it with school work.

After applying to some 10 to 15 jobs and internships, Charles had heard back from a few places by mid-May, and got interviews with some of them.

"It does take some time going through the process," she said. "Especially when you're trying to graduate from college."

Temple senior Mario Pacheco, who studies mechanical engineering, hopes networking will make him stand out from other applicants. He has one course to finish this fall, but plans to ramp up his efforts to get a full-time job by the time he's done.

In-person networking is all the more important right now, said Kebea from Campus Philly, partly because hiring managers are flooded with applicants.

Pacheco is also working on getting an engineer certification to beef up his resumé.

"I'm just trying to stay as positive as possible, and trying to do as much as I can to distinguish myself from other graduates," said Pacheco.

He's spending the summer interning with the Philadelphia Housing Authority, as he did last year. For 30 hours a week and $17 an hour, he worked on HVAC systems at PHA sites.

"There's always buildings going up that need HVAC systems designed," he said. "There's a chance for there to be plenty of work in that field."

Employers like IBM and McKinsey are hiring more entry-level positions this year, but those roles are changing with the adoption of AI. The technology is also making some young workers rethink their career paths.

"AI can automate tasks, but it doesn't develop people and the talent that we need," said Kebea. If AI leads to fewer entry-level opportunities, Kebea noted, that means fewer people are getting trained in those early jobs, creating a talent shortage in the long term.

For the time being, employers are looking to hire people who know how to use AI and can hit the ground running, said Kebea.

Jiang, the Drexel senior, has used AI in past workplaces, with her employers' blessing, to help create prompts on social media including LinkedIn. She also used AI to refine her resumé.

Some college students have trepidations around how AI is being used to screen job candidates, Kebea said, but she noted that employers have been using hiring technology to screen applicants for some time. While young people may be tempted to apply to many more jobs in the age of AI, she recommends against it.

"It's not a numbers game. It's a quality game," said Kebea.

Students are both ambitious and anxious in today's job market, said Kebea, but many are rising to the occasion.

"Gen Z is so pragmatic," she said. "They're absolutely still ambitious about their potential in the workforce."

In April, Soesanto, the biology graduate at Drexel, got an offer he couldn't refuse.

He was running on the Delaware River Trail when he saw an alert on his phone: He was the recipient of a Fulbright award - the prestigious grant to work or teach abroad.

"I was just mind blown, really stoked, really happy, euphoric," said Soesanto, who in early May was planning to accept.

In September he'll start 10 months of research in Indonesia studying the symbiosis of a species of fish and their bacteria. The project "is what I've wanted to do for the longest time," he said, but he's also accepting the offer because of the challenge of landing a job right now.

"It takes a while to get a job," said Soesanto. "There's an open door for me, and I'd rather take that one."

news_list.title: Nissan Is Fighting For Survival. It Just Placed Two Big Bets. - AOL
news_list.summary:
This time last year, Nissan CEO Ivan Espinoza had that deer in the headlights look. And no wonder. He'd just taken the top job at Japan's second-largest automaker, and the company was in deep trouble. Worldwide sales were 40 percent lower than they had been a mere eight years earlier, and losses for the 2024 financial year totaled $4.5 billion. A proposed merger with Honda had been called off, and Nissan was now said to be worth barely four percent as much as its long-time archrival Toyota. An unnamed senior executive had reckoned the company had just 12 to 14 months left to survive.

Of course, none of this was a surprise for Espinoza, then a 22-year Nissan veteran whose previous role at the company was as chief planning officer. But the enormity of the task ahead was daunting. Espinoza was targeting $3.4 billion in cost reductions by closing seven of Nissan's 17 factories worldwide, reducing its total number of platforms from 13 to seven, and cutting its workforce by 15 percent. All work on new models scheduled for launch after 2026 had been temporarily paused, with 3,000 staff reportedly moved to work on reducing parts complexity and redundancy by 70 percent.

It's been a tough year since then. But Nissan is still here. Today, Espinoza says the company's Re:Nissan turnaround strategy has already cut fixed costs by $1.3 billion and variable costs by $350 million. Global sales are still slow -- Nissan finished 2025 having sold 3.15 million vehicles worldwide, well down from the 5.77 million it sold in 2017 -- but Nissan's boss believes the company now has a foundation on which to grow. His target is to get worldwide sales up to 3.3 million vehicles by the end of this year. "It's growth, but I will qualify it as prudent," he told media and analysts at the recent Financial Times Future of the Car summit in London.

As they have for decades, Japan and the U.S. will remain the bedrock of Nissan's global business going forward. But to survive -- to grow -- Espinoza believes Nissan needs to develop and manufacture more vehicles in China and invest heavily in embedding AI capability in all its vehicles.

Like all Japanese automakers, as well as and European and American mainstream brands, Nissan has struggled to gain the volumes it expected as the Chinese auto market has grown. But four new vehicles developed in conjunction with its Chinese partner Dongfeng are beginning to increase Nissan's sales in what is now the world's largest and most ruthlessly competitive automotive market.

The Nissan N7 is an EV sedan larger than the Altima, with a 3.6-inch longer wheelbase; it's powered by a 215-hp or 268-hp single electric motor that drives the front wheels and is fed by a 58-kWh or 73-kWh battery pack. The N6 is a plug-in hybrid front-wheel-drive sedan slightly smaller than the Altima that has a 101-hp 1.5-liter four-cylinder internal combustion engine augmented by a 208-hp e-motor under the hood.

The Nissan NX8 is a rear-drive SUV sized between the Rogue and the Pathfinder and available as either an EV with 288 or 335 hp, or as an extended-range EV (EREV) with a 146-hp 1.5-liter four-cylinder engine acting as a generator for the 261-hp motor at the rear axle. Nissan says the NX8 has a pure electric driving range of 193 miles, or 900 miles with the internal combustion engine in operation.

The Frontier Pro pickup shares a name with its U.S. counterpart, but that's all. This Chinese-made truck is available as a plug-in hybrid with a 1.5-liter four-cylinder internal combustion engine and a motor that combine to make 402 hp and 590 lb-ft of torque, outputs that easily shade the 310 hp and 268 lb-ft produced by the 3.8-liter V-6 under the hood of the U.S.-market Frontier built in Canton, Mississippi.

"China is a difficult market," Espinoza admits, "but the from the moment we started to bring product that has been designed specifically for the Chinese customer we have seen growth." In the first quarter of this year, Nissan sales in China were seven percent up year on the same quarter last year. "This is proof that we have competitive products," Espinoza says. "We know how to make exciting cars, and we know how to design cars for customers."

And not just customers in China. As Nissan works on closing plants in Japan, Mexico, and Europe, it is looking to increase exports of its Chinese-made vehicles to 300,000 per year. Potential markets for Chinese-made Nissans identified by Espinoza include Latin America, Southeast Asia, and the Middle East, all markets that, ironically, once exclusively bought Nissans made in Japan.

And though Espinoza didn't call them out, the low tariffs on Chinese vehicles in Canada and the U.K. -- the Chinese-made Jaecoo J7 SUV was Britain's bestselling vehicle in March -- make both countries potential export targets as well. "Even in China, where there is a very severe price war, we are profitable with these vehicles," Espinoza says. "So, when we export these cars we can have a good business."

But the real future for Nissan, Espinoza says, is affordable AI-powered autonomous vehicles, both for use by private customers and by robotaxi companies. Nissan's 'Mobility Intelligence for Everyday Life', a strategic vision announced by Espinoza in April, says the coming generation of Nissans will be AI Defined Vehicles (AIDVs). "Our ambition is to get up to 90 percent of our volume [equipped] with this technology," he says.

Nissan recently signed an agreement with British-based AI startup Wayve to embed its AI software into its ProPilot driver assistance system, which already enables Level 2++ autonomous driving capability under certain conditions. The AI-enhanced ProPIilot is expected to debut on the new Elgrand minivan due for launch in Japan this summer and be able to support advanced point-to-point autonomous driving capability by late 2027.

Beyond that, Espinoza wants AI to power a new generation of in-car experiences for future Nissan customers. "Customers will be sitting in their cars when they have long commutes, so what can we offer them?" he asks. "What kind of value can we bring to their lives while they are in our cars, looking at our screens for 45 minutes or one hour every day?" Espinoza envisions a subscription model in which owners have access to multiple services created by Nissan and other partners, an ecosystem that will provide services and experiences related to productivity or entertainment. "There are so many things that you can do with technology today and this is how we are going to start building a strong business model," he says.

Nissan will begin testing robotaxis in Japan later this year. "We want to be an active player in this field," he says, "not only by providing the car, but also by providing support through all the value chain. We have dealers and we have infrastructure in terms of spare parts warehousing. We can service the cars. We can invest in technology to make the robotaxi operators more efficient, like having AI-based charging schedules so that you can optimize the energy costs of their fleet." He also sees robodelivery services becoming a profitable business. "There are a lot of companies worldwide that would require or be interested in having [their] delivery services running automated and autonomous cars," he says.

Espinoza believes Nissan can be the leader among Japanese automakers when it comes to intelligent and autonomous vehicles, finally giving the brand a clear point of difference compared to Toyota or Honda. "We have the technology and we have the credentials," he says. "We are the most advanced Japanese OEM in autonomous drive technology, and we have a very strong position in terms of EV technology as well as hybrid technology. These things are the foundation of the intelligent car, which is the future."

news_list.title: Fed's Jefferson says monetary policy is well positioned to respond, not prejudge June meet | investingLive
news_list.summary:
Fed's Jefferson says policy well positioned but flags upside inflation risks

Fed Vice Chair Jefferson says monetary policy is well positioned to respond to developments but has not prejudged June's FOMC meeting, flagging upside inflation risks and energy shock exposure.

Summary: Source: Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson, speech to the 2026 Bank of Japan-Institute for Monetary and Economic Studies Conference in Tokyo, 27 May 2026

Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said on Wednesday that monetary policy is well positioned to respond to whatever the economy delivers, while stopping short of any signal on the direction of the next move and explicitly leaving the outcome of June's rate-setting meeting open.

Jefferson delivered the remarks in a speech to the 2026 Bank of Japan-Institute for Monetary and Economic Studies Conference in Tokyo, his first public comments since Kevin Warsh was sworn in as Fed chair last Friday, succeeding Jerome Powell, who remains at the central bank as a governor.

The current federal funds rate range of 3.50% to 3.75%, Jefferson said, gives the Fed the flexibility it needs to respond to incoming data and the evolving balance of risks. On the June 16-17 Federal Open Market Committee meeting, he was deliberate about keeping options open, saying he had not prejudged the outcome and was looking forward to engaging with colleagues on the policy path best suited to achieving the Fed's dual mandate.

Jefferson placed inflation squarely at the centre of his risk assessment. He said risks to the inflation outlook are tilted to the upside and reaffirmed his commitment to returning inflation to the 2% target. He does expect price pressures to ease later in the year as the impact of tariffs and energy costs fades, but he was careful to frame that as a baseline rather than a certainty.

On energy, Jefferson acknowledged directly that the United States, despite being a substantial domestic producer, is not fully insulated from the disruptions the Iran war (latest ceasefire breach here) has created in global oil markets. He described the energy shock as a downside risk to growth and an upside risk to inflation, a two-sided assessment that reflects the bind facing policymakers as the conflict in the Middle East continues.

On the broader economy, Jefferson's assessment was measured. Recent economic activity has been solid and the labor market stable, characterised by low rates of both hiring and firing. However, he noted that risks to employment are tilted to the downside, a signal consistent with the cautious tone other Fed officials have struck this week, including Governor Cook, who also flagged labor market vulnerability in her remarks on Wednesday.

Warsh, who expressed interest in cutting rates as he pursued the Fed chair role, is widely expected to face difficulty delivering any reduction this year given persistent inflation pressures tied to import tariffs and the war.

--

Jefferson's comments reinforce the broader Fed message that has emerged this week: the current rate setting is appropriate for now, but the bar for cuts is high and a hike remains a live option if inflation does not cooperate. His explicit acknowledgment that the US is not immune to oil-related energy shocks ties Fed policy directly to Hormuz developments, giving crude price moves an additional read-through to rate expectations. The deliberate non-commitment on June adds no pressure in either direction, leaving the meeting genuinely open data dependent.

Students are both ambitious and anxious in today's job market, said Kebea, but many are rising to the occasion.

"Gen Z is so pragmatic," she said. "They're absolutely still ambitious about their potential in the workforce."

In April, Soesanto, the biology graduate at Drexel, got an offer he couldn't refuse.

He was running on the Delaware River Trail when he saw an alert on his phone: He was the recipient of a Fulbright award - the prestigious grant to work or teach abroad.

"I was just mind blown, really stoked, really happy, euphoric," said Soesanto, who in early May was planning to accept.

In September he'll start 10 months of research in Indonesia studying the symbiosis of a species of fish and their bacteria. The project "is what I've wanted to do for the longest time," he said, but he's also accepting the offer because of the challenge of landing a job right now.

"It takes a while to get a job," said Soesanto. "There's an open door for me, and I'd rather take that one."

items.title: Nissan Is Fighting For Survival. It Just Placed Two Big Bets. - AOL
items.summary:
This time last year, Nissan CEO Ivan Espinoza had that deer in the headlights look. And no wonder. He'd just taken the top job at Japan's second-largest automaker, and the company was in deep trouble. Worldwide sales were 40 percent lower than they had been a mere eight years earlier, and losses for the 2024 financial year totaled $4.5 billion. A proposed merger with Honda had been called off, and Nissan was now said to be worth barely four percent as much as its long-time archrival Toyota. An unnamed senior executive had reckoned the company had just 12 to 14 months left to survive.

Of course, none of this was a surprise for Espinoza, then a 22-year Nissan veteran whose previous role at the company was as chief planning officer. But the enormity of the task ahead was daunting. Espinoza was targeting $3.4 billion in cost reductions by closing seven of Nissan's 17 factories worldwide, reducing its total number of platforms from 13 to seven, and cutting its workforce by 15 percent. All work on new models scheduled for launch after 2026 had been temporarily paused, with 3,000 staff reportedly moved to work on reducing parts complexity and redundancy by 70 percent.

It's been a tough year since then. But Nissan is still here. Today, Espinoza says the company's Re:Nissan turnaround strategy has already cut fixed costs by $1.3 billion and variable costs by $350 million. Global sales are still slow -- Nissan finished 2025 having sold 3.15 million vehicles worldwide, well down from the 5.77 million it sold in 2017 -- but Nissan's boss believes the company now has a foundation on which to grow. His target is to get worldwide sales up to 3.3 million vehicles by the end of this year. "It's growth, but I will qualify it as prudent," he told media and analysts at the recent Financial Times Future of the Car summit in London.

As they have for decades, Japan and the U.S. will remain the bedrock of Nissan's global business going forward. But to survive -- to grow -- Espinoza believes Nissan needs to develop and manufacture more vehicles in China and invest heavily in embedding AI capability in all its vehicles.

Like all Japanese automakers, as well as and European and American mainstream brands, Nissan has struggled to gain the volumes it expected as the Chinese auto market has grown. But four new vehicles developed in conjunction with its Chinese partner Dongfeng are beginning to increase Nissan's sales in what is now the world's largest and most ruthlessly competitive automotive market.

The Nissan N7 is an EV sedan larger than the Altima, with a 3.6-inch longer wheelbase; it's powered by a 215-hp or 268-hp single electric motor that drives the front wheels and is fed by a 58-kWh or 73-kWh battery pack. The N6 is a plug-in hybrid front-wheel-drive sedan slightly smaller than the Altima that has a 101-hp 1.5-liter four-cylinder internal combustion engine augmented by a 208-hp e-motor under the hood.

The Nissan NX8 is a rear-drive SUV sized between the Rogue and the Pathfinder and available as either an EV with 288 or 335 hp, or as an extended-range EV (EREV) with a 146-hp 1.5-liter four-cylinder engine acting as a generator for the 261-hp motor at the rear axle. Nissan says the NX8 has a pure electric driving range of 193 miles, or 900 miles with the internal combustion engine in operation.

The Frontier Pro pickup shares a name with its U.S. counterpart, but that's all. This Chinese-made truck is available as a plug-in hybrid with a 1.5-liter four-cylinder internal combustion engine and a motor that combine to make 402 hp and 590 lb-ft of torque, outputs that easily shade the 310 hp and 268 lb-ft produced by the 3.8-liter V-6 under the hood of the U.S.-market Frontier built in Canton, Mississippi.

"China is a difficult market," Espinoza admits, "but the from the moment we started to bring product that has been designed specifically for the Chinese customer we have seen growth." In the first quarter of this year, Nissan sales in China were seven percent up year on the same quarter last year. "This is proof that we have competitive products," Espinoza says. "We know how to make exciting cars, and we know how to design cars for customers."

And not just customers in China. As Nissan works on closing plants in Japan, Mexico, and Europe, it is looking to increase exports of its Chinese-made vehicles to 300,000 per year. Potential markets for Chinese-made Nissans identified by Espinoza include Latin America, Southeast Asia, and the Middle East, all markets that, ironically, once exclusively bought Nissans made in Japan.

And though Espinoza didn't call them out, the low tariffs on Chinese vehicles in Canada and the U.K. -- the Chinese-made Jaecoo J7 SUV was Britain's bestselling vehicle in March -- make both countries potential export targets as well. "Even in China, where there is a very severe price war, we are profitable with these vehicles," Espinoza says. "So, when we export these cars we can have a good business."

But the real future for Nissan, Espinoza says, is affordable AI-powered autonomous vehicles, both for use by private customers and by robotaxi companies. Nissan's 'Mobility Intelligence for Everyday Life', a strategic vision announced by Espinoza in April, says the coming generation of Nissans will be AI Defined Vehicles (AIDVs). "Our ambition is to get up to 90 percent of our volume [equipped] with this technology," he says.

Nissan recently signed an agreement with British-based AI startup Wayve to embed its AI software into its ProPilot driver assistance system, which already enables Level 2++ autonomous driving capability under certain conditions. The AI-enhanced ProPIilot is expected to debut on the new Elgrand minivan due for launch in Japan this summer and be able to support advanced point-to-point autonomous driving capability by late 2027.

Beyond that, Espinoza wants AI to power a new generation of in-car experiences for future Nissan customers. "Customers will be sitting in their cars when they have long commutes, so what can we offer them?" he asks. "What kind of value can we bring to their lives while they are in our cars, looking at our screens for 45 minutes or one hour every day?" Espinoza envisions a subscription model in which owners have access to multiple services created by Nissan and other partners, an ecosystem that will provide services and experiences related to productivity or entertainment. "There are so many things that you can do with technology today and this is how we are going to start building a strong business model," he says.

Nissan will begin testing robotaxis in Japan later this year. "We want to be an active player in this field," he says, "not only by providing the car, but also by providing support through all the value chain. We have dealers and we have infrastructure in terms of spare parts warehousing. We can service the cars. We can invest in technology to make the robotaxi operators more efficient, like having AI-based charging schedules so that you can optimize the energy costs of their fleet." He also sees robodelivery services becoming a profitable business. "There are a lot of companies worldwide that would require or be interested in having [their] delivery services running automated and autonomous cars," he says.

Espinoza believes Nissan can be the leader among Japanese automakers when it comes to intelligent and autonomous vehicles, finally giving the brand a clear point of difference compared to Toyota or Honda. "We have the technology and we have the credentials," he says. "We are the most advanced Japanese OEM in autonomous drive technology, and we have a very strong position in terms of EV technology as well as hybrid technology. These things are the foundation of the intelligent car, which is the future."

items.title: Fed's Jefferson says monetary policy is well positioned to respond, not prejudge June meet | investingLive
items.summary:
Fed's Jefferson says policy well positioned but flags upside inflation risks

Fed Vice Chair Jefferson says monetary policy is well positioned to respond to developments but has not prejudged June's FOMC meeting, flagging upside inflation risks and energy shock exposure.

Summary: Source: Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson, speech to the 2026 Bank of Japan-Institute for Monetary and Economic Studies Conference in Tokyo, 27 May 2026

Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said on Wednesday that monetary policy is well positioned to respond to whatever the economy delivers, while stopping short of any signal on the direction of the next move and explicitly leaving the outcome of June's rate-setting meeting open.

Jefferson delivered the remarks in a speech to the 2026 Bank of Japan-Institute for Monetary and Economic Studies Conference in Tokyo, his first public comments since Kevin Warsh was sworn in as Fed chair last Friday, succeeding Jerome Powell, who remains at the central bank as a governor.

The current federal funds rate range of 3.50% to 3.75%, Jefferson said, gives the Fed the flexibility it needs to respond to incoming data and the evolving balance of risks. On the June 16-17 Federal Open Market Committee meeting, he was deliberate about keeping options open, saying he had not prejudged the outcome and was looking forward to engaging with colleagues on the policy path best suited to achieving the Fed's dual mandate.

Jefferson placed inflation squarely at the centre of his risk assessment. He said risks to the inflation outlook are tilted to the upside and reaffirmed his commitment to returning inflation to the 2% target. He does expect price pressures to ease later in the year as the impact of tariffs and energy costs fades, but he was careful to frame that as a baseline rather than a certainty.

On energy, Jefferson acknowledged directly that the United States, despite being a substantial domestic producer, is not fully insulated from the disruptions the Iran war (latest ceasefire breach here) has created in global oil markets. He described the energy shock as a downside risk to growth and an upside risk to inflation, a two-sided assessment that reflects the bind facing policymakers as the conflict in the Middle East continues.

On the broader economy, Jefferson's assessment was measured. Recent economic activity has been solid and the labor market stable, characterised by low rates of both hiring and firing. However, he noted that risks to employment are tilted to the downside, a signal consistent with the cautious tone other Fed officials have struck this week, including Governor Cook, who also flagged labor market vulnerability in her remarks on Wednesday.

Warsh, who expressed interest in cutting rates as he pursued the Fed chair role, is widely expected to face difficulty delivering any reduction this year given persistent inflation pressures tied to import tariffs and the war.

--

Jefferson's comments reinforce the broader Fed message that has emerged this week: the current rate setting is appropriate for now, but the bar for cuts is high and a hike remains a live option if inflation does not cooperate. His explicit acknowledgment that the US is not immune to oil-related energy shocks ties Fed policy directly to Hormuz developments, giving crude price moves an additional read-through to rate expectations. The deliberate non-commitment on June adds no pressure in either direction, leaving the meeting genuinely open data dependent.

ai_analysis.full_text:
【今日結論】
今天（28日）台股將是開高後的多空拉鋸盤。主要的多方動能來自台積電ADR昨夜大漲2.52%，換算溢價高達15.64%，將強勢帶動大盤開高；然而，費城半導體指數拉回1.36%，顯示AI內部已出現分歧，加上鷹派的聯準會言論，將壓抑追價力道，預期指數開高後將在高檔震盪，呈現權值股撐盤、中小型股各自表現的格局。
【新聞驅動】
市場對AI的敘事正在從全面樂觀轉向個股分化。儘管Salesforce財報亮眼，但市場更關注AI資本支出是否侵蝕股東回報，這解釋了為何Nasdaq創新高、但費城半導體指數卻明顯拉回。同時，聯準會理事庫克重申不排除升息的鷹派立場，加上中東地緣政治風險，為市場的非理性繁榮提供了清醒劑，高估值的AI股將面臨更嚴格的檢視。
【國際與台股】
今日台股將上演「一座神山對抗全球逆風」的戲碼。最強支撐是台積電ADR的強勁表現與富台期指夜盤大漲2.27%，顯示外資對台灣龍頭股的偏好未減；但最大的壓力來自費半指數的逆風，以及日經、韓股早盤同步走弱的區域性賣壓。這種矛盾訊號意味著，資金將高度集中在台積電及其供應鏈，而非全面性的上漲，盤中需關注除了半導體外的資金流向，以判斷市場真實的強度。
【KOL與情緒】
社群與KOL的觀點已出現嚴重分歧，市場進入高檔的「決策雜訊區」。一派認為AI趨勢銳不可擋，任何拉回都是買點；另一派則警告市場已陷入脫離現實的FOMO狂熱，是絕佳的反向操作時機。這種多空論述的極化，加上散戶熱衷於高股息ETF（如00919）與股東會題材（如群創），顯示部分資金正從追逐動能轉向尋求確定性，市場在高檔的換手與分歧正在加劇。
【操作含意】
操作上應採取「順勢操作，但嚴控追價風險」的策略。今日開盤跳空是可預期的，但不應在開盤第一時間追高，核心觀察點在於開盤後，買盤是否從台積電擴散至其他AI概念股與電子族群。若指數開高後，僅靠台積電獨撐，而中小型股卻出現賣壓（即所謂的「拉積盤」），則應視為風險升高的訊號，須減碼或將資金轉進防禦型標的。
